cim: Leadership: Judgment, Purpose, and Human Responsibility
cim_eredeti: Leadership: Judgment, Purpose, and Human Responsibility
szoveg_eredeti:
Leadership in the age of artificial intelligence does not depend solely on knowing how to use new tools, but on developing self-awareness, critical thinking, and the judgment to decide what can be automated and what must remain under human responsibility. Ruth Gamero reflects on credibility, curiosity, career development, self-management, and purpose as the pillars of leadership in an environment marked by rapid technological advancement. Her approach links the use of AI to a fundamental question: technology can expand our capabilities, but it is up to people to guide its application and accept its consequences. Facilitating meaningful and responsible access to digital technologies also requires leaders capable of integrating innovation and values, harnessing the potential of artificial intelligence, and maintaining human oversight when decisions involve ambiguity, risk, or an impact that is difficult to reverse.

Leadership in the age of artificial intelligence requires self-awareness, sound judgment, and purpose to harness technology without delegating human responsibility for decisions and their consequences.

In an age when artificial intelligence can offer us more and more answers, what do we need to learn about ourselves in order to make good choices? This question connects to an ancient inscription on the Temple of Apollo at Delphi—“Know thyself”—which we can apply to modern leadership as a call to understand our capabilities, recognize our limits, and examine the motivations that guide our decisions.

When we talk about leadership, we tend to think of leading teams, driving change, defining strategies, or mobilizing organizations. However, there is a prerequisite that we often overlook: before leading others, we must learn to lead ourselves. This involves knowing ourselves, choosing how to act, and accepting the consequences of our decisions.

AI can help us analyze, draft, and explore alternatives, but defining our purpose, deciding what deserves our attention, and assessing the impact of our actions still requires human judgment. That judgment needs more than just information: it requires an awareness of who we are, what drives us, and what biases might shape our perspective.

The Delphic maxim thus takes on concrete meaning in the age of AI: the more we rely on tools capable of generating answers, the more important it becomes to understand where our questions come from and why we accept some conclusions while rejecting others. Leadership is built on this ability to know ourselves, manage ourselves, and grow consciously.

If leadership is the ability to influence others, credibility is its foundation. That credibility stems from the consistency between what we think, say, and do, and it sustains trust. Marcus Aurelius expresses this requirement in his Meditations: “If it is not right, do not do it; if it is not true, do not say it.” Applied to leadership, this teaching links the integrity of our actions to the honesty of our words: fulfilling commitments, communicating transparently, and acting in accordance with the principles we uphold.

Today, that trust takes on special importance in a global environment often described through two frameworks: VUCA and BANI.

VUCA refers to the volatility, uncertainty, complexity, and ambiguity of an environment where change is accelerating, the future is difficult to anticipate, factors are interconnected, and a single situation can be interpreted in different ways.

BANI adds another perspective: fragility, anxiety, non-linearity, and incomprehensibility. It describes seemingly solid systems that can break down, situations that create uncertainty when making decisions, small causes with disproportionate consequences, and phenomena that remain difficult to understand even when we have abundant information.

In this context, Marcus Aurelius’ reflections offer useful guidance: to examine our judgments and act in a reasoned manner. In the Meditations, he also advises pausing and seeking out good advisors when we lack clarity. Applied to modern leadership, this means acknowledging our doubts and drawing on the wisdom of others before making a decision.

It’s tempting to seek an immediate answer to every problem, especially when AI can provide one in seconds. However, a convincing answer may prematurely shut down a reasoning process that needed further questions.

Leadership also requires recognizing when we know enough to act and when it is better to pause, listen, or seek second opinions. Self-awareness helps us distinguish whether we are making sound decisions or reacting to pressure, fear, or our own biases. Credibility is also built on this ability to recognize our limits and act responsibly.

Curiosity is one of the roots of leadership: the drive to learn, to understand the world around us, and to maintain an attitude of continuous growth. Aristotle opens his Metaphysics with a statement that connects to this idea: “All human beings by nature desire to know.” Applied to leadership, this idea invites us to cultivate the desire to understand and to remain open to what we do not yet know.

People who take charge of their own lives nurture that curiosity. They observe, listen, connect ideas, and seek new perspectives. They ask questions and are willing to reevaluate their certainties. They understand that knowledge is a journey in which every discovery can open up new possibilities for learning.

In an environment marked by rapid technological advancement and artificial intelligence, the ability to learn is especially valuable. But learning requires more than just accumulating information: it means developing discernment, distinguishing what is relevant from what is incidental, and understanding the implications of the answers we receive. AI can expand our capacity to explore; curiosity drives us to delve deeper, cross-check, and ask why.

Keeping our capacity for wonder alive is also a form of self-leadership. It allows us to recognize the limits of what we know, question our assumptions, and continue to grow. The desire for knowledge that Aristotle spoke of thus becomes a daily practice: learning with an open mind and using what we’ve learned to make better decisions.

There is a tendency to measure professional success through job titles, responsibilities, or visible achievements. However, over time, one discovers that a true professional career is not just about what you do, but the person you become while doing it.

Every project, every change in role, every challenge, and every transition leaves a mark. It all adds up. Nothing is lost. Experiences come together and ultimately shape a broader view of the world and of ourselves.

That’s why, rather than pursuing a linear path, it’s better to develop the ability to evolve. It’s not about changing just for the sake of change. It’s about knowing how to recognize when the time has come to learn something new, broaden your horizons, or reinvent yourself.

Personal leadership is based precisely on that: on knowing how to read the context and listen to what our own evolution is asking of us.

Artificial intelligence is going to profoundly transform the way we work. Many tasks will be automated, and many decisions will be supported by intelligent systems. Precisely for this reason, the most human skills will become increasingly valuable: critical thinking, creativity, complex judgment, empathy, communication, active listening, and the ability to work as a team. And, of course, leadership.

It is not enough to simply master technology or focus exclusively on human capabilities. The future requires integrating both worlds and developing the necessary discernment to decide what we can delegate to artificial intelligence, what we must oversee, and which responsibilities must remain essentially human.
